title: What is Project Skara — the OpenJDK project that migrated the JDK source code from Mercurial to Git and built tooling (bots, CLI tools, and GitHub/GitLab integrations) to modernize OpenJDK's code review and contribution workflow — and why does it matter for contributors (lower barrier to entry, familiar PR-based workflow, faster review cycles)?
shortTitle: What is Project Skara and why does it matter for contributors?

s1_definition.profdef: Project Skara is the OpenJDK project that modernized how the JDK source code is stored and how contributions are reviewed. It migrated the JDK codebase from Mercurial to Git, moved the repositories to GitHub, and built the automation that makes a pull-request-based workflow work under OpenJDK's governance rules. This automation includes bots that enforce contributor agreements and reviewer rules, that integrate with the JDK Bug System and the JEP process, and that perform the actual integration into the mainline, plus CLI tools and GitHub and GitLab integrations. It matters for contributors because it lowers the barrier to entry, offers the familiar pull-request workflow millions of developers already know, and speeds up review cycles.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India used to accept new policy proposals only by posting handwritten letters to a central office using an old, unusual postal system that few people understood, where every letter had to be formatted in a very particular way or it was rejected. Project Skara is like the bank switching to a modern, well-known submission portal that almost every professional already knows how to use, with helpful assistants that automatically check your submission meets the rules, attach the right case numbers, and route it to the correct reviewers. Nothing about the bank's strict approval standards changed, but far more people can now contribute, and proposals move through review faster because the clerical work is automated.
s1_definition.oneliner: Project Skara moved the JDK from Mercurial to Git on GitHub and built the bots and tooling that make a familiar pull-request workflow work under OpenJDK's rules, lowering the barrier to contribute and speeding up reviews.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Project Skara is the OpenJDK project that modernized how the JDK source code is stored and how contributions are reviewed. It migrated the JDK codebase from Mercurial to Git, moved the repositories to GitHub, and built the automation that makes a pull-request-based workflow work under OpenJDK's governance rules. This automation includes bots that enforce contributor agreements and reviewer rules, that integrate with the JDK Bug System and the JEP process, and that perform the actual integration into the mainline, plus CLI tools and GitHub and GitLab integrations. It matters for contributors because it lowers the barrier to entry, offers the familiar pull-request workflow millions of developers already know, and speeds up review cycles.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India used to accept new policy proposals only by posting handwritten letters to a central office using an old, unusual postal system that few people understood, where every letter had to be formatted in a very particular way or it was rejected. Project Skara is like the bank switching to a modern, well-known submission portal that almost every professional already knows how to use, with helpful assistants that automatically check your submission meets the rules, attach the right case numbers, and route it to the correct reviewers. Nothing about the bank's strict approval standards changed, but far more people can now contribute, and proposals move through review faster because the clerical work is automated.

**One line to remember:** Project Skara moved the JDK from Mercurial to Git on GitHub and built the bots and tooling that make a familiar pull-request workflow work under OpenJDK's rules, lowering the barrier to contribute and speeding up reviews.

sections.s2_technical:
Before Skara, OpenJDK development used Mercurial, a distributed version control system that is perfectly capable but far less widely used than Git. The code review process relied on mailing lists and webrev, a tool that generated static HTML diffs that you posted for reviewers to comment on by email. This workflow was unfamiliar to most developers, had a steep learning curve, and the mechanics of submitting a change, getting it reviewed, and having it integrated were manual and idiosyncratic. The result was a high barrier to entry that discouraged casual and new contributors.

Project Skara changed three things. First, it migrated the source from Mercurial to Git. Git is the de facto standard, so contributors already know how to clone, branch, commit, and rebase. Second, it moved the repositories to GitHub, which brings the pull-request model, inline review comments, status checks, and a familiar web interface. Third, and most importantly, it built the automation that reconciles the open GitHub workflow with OpenJDK's strict governance, because OpenJDK cannot simply accept any pull request; it has legal and process requirements that must be enforced.

That automation is a set of bots, often collectively called the Skara bots. When you open a pull request against an OpenJDK repository, a bot checks that you have signed the Oracle Contributor Agreement or are otherwise authorized, because contributions must be legally clean. A bot verifies the change references a valid issue in the JDK Bug System, since every change is tracked by a bug or enhancement id, and it links the pull request to that issue. A bot enforces the reviewer rules, confirming that the required number of qualified reviewers, identified by their OpenJDK roles, have approved, because different areas of the JDK require specific reviewer counts and expertise. The bot also runs the commit-message and whitespace checks that OpenJDK mandates. When all conditions are satisfied, the author issues an integrate command as a comment, and the bot performs the actual merge into the mainline, creating a properly formatted commit that preserves OpenJDK's history conventions. There is also a sponsor flow where a committer sponsors a non-committer's change.

Skara also produced CLI tools, the git-jcheck and related commands and the git-webrev replacement, so contributors can run the same checks locally before pushing, and it provides integrations so the workflow can function on GitHub and GitLab. It preserved the ability to still interact through familiar means while modernizing the plumbing.

Why does this matter for contributors? The barrier to entry dropped dramatically because a developer who already knows Git and GitHub can contribute to the JDK using skills they already have, instead of learning Mercurial, webrev, and mailing-list etiquette first. The pull-request workflow gives inline, threaded review comments and a clear status of what checks pass and what reviews are needed, which is far more approachable than email threads. Review cycles got faster because the bots automate the clerical gatekeeping, the contributor agreement check, the issue linking, the reviewer counting, and the integration, so human reviewers spend their time on the actual code rather than on process bookkeeping. The net effect is a healthier, more open contribution funnel for the world's most important runtime.

A senior framing: Skara is not a language or runtime feature, so it does not change how your Java code behaves at all. It is infrastructure and process modernization. But it matters strategically, because the long-term health of Java depends on being able to attract and retain contributors, and a modern, familiar, automated workflow is a major part of that. When an interviewer asks about Skara, they are testing whether you understand the OpenJDK ecosystem and governance, not just the language.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a large internal shared-libraries platform, and for years changes were submitted through an obscure, manual process that most engineers found intimidating, so only a handful of experts ever contributed, and reviews dragged on for weeks. This is exactly the pre-Skara OpenJDK situation: an unfamiliar workflow and manual gatekeeping choke the contribution funnel.

Problem 2 — The platform team wanted to lower the barrier so any bank engineer could propose a change using the Git and pull-request skills they already have, while still enforcing the bank's strict rules: a signed contributor agreement, a linked change-ticket, and a required number of senior reviewers before merge. This is exactly what the Skara bots do for OpenJDK, reconcile an open pull-request workflow with strict governance through automation.

Problem 3 — Reviewers were spending their time on clerical checks instead of code. This is the automation win: bots should enforce the agreement, link the ticket, and count reviewers, freeing humans for the code.

Since Skara itself is infrastructure, the mini-project models the idea it embodies: a small contribution-gate engine that, like the Skara bots, checks a proposed change against the rules before allowing integration. We model a change to a banking library proposed by an engineer, and the gate verifies agreement, ticket link, and reviewer count, then integrates. Characters Rajesh and Priya appear as contributor and reviewer.

The code contains: a `Contribution` record; a `ContributionGate` that mimics the bot checks; and a runnable demo that submits a change and integrates it when rules pass.

java -cp out com.bank.contrib.GateDemo

# Real Skara interaction is via git + GitHub PR comments, for example:

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three proposed changes to the bank's shared library, modeling three OpenJDK pull requests with different states.

Step 1: Rajesh's change arrives with the agreement signed, a linked ticket NBI-1234, and one approval from Priya. This mirrors a clean OpenJDK pull request.

Step 2: `integrate` calls `canIntegrate`. The agreement check passes because Rajesh signed. The issue-link check passes because NBI-1234 is present. The reviewer-count check passes because one reviewer, Priya, approved, meeting the required count.

Step 3: Because all rules pass, the gate performs the integration and logs that change NBI-1234 by Rajesh was integrated, approved by Priya. This is the bot executing the integrate command.

Step 4: The second change, by a new joiner, has not signed the agreement. The agreement check fails immediately, and the gate blocks integration with a clear reason, exactly as a Skara bot refuses a pull request lacking a signed contributor agreement.

Step 5: The third change, by Rajesh, is well-formed but has zero approvals. The reviewer-count check fails, and integration is refused until a reviewer approves, mirroring OpenJDK's reviewer rules.

Step 6: The outcomes show the key idea: an open, familiar submission path, but strict automated governance before anything merges.

```
Oct 26, 2026 3:47:10 PM com.bank.contrib.service.ContributionGate integrate
INFO: Integrated change NBI-1234 by Rajesh (approved by [Priya])
Oct 26, 2026 3:47:10 PM com.bank.contrib.service.ContributionGate canIntegrate
WARNING: Blocked: NewJoiner has not signed the contributor agreement
Oct 26, 2026 3:47:10 PM com.bank.contrib.service.ContributionGate integrate
SEVERE: Integration refused for change by NewJoiner
Oct 26, 2026 3:47:10 PM com.bank.contrib.service.ContributionGate canIntegrate
WARNING: Blocked: needs 1 reviewer(s), has 0
Oct 26, 2026 3:47:10 PM com.bank.contrib.service.ContributionGate integrate
SEVERE: Integration refused for change by Rajesh
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Contributor (Rajesh) opens a change (like a GitHub Pull Request)
    │
    ▼
  ContributionGate  (≈ Skara bots)
    │
    ├─ agreement signed?  ──no──→ BLOCK ("sign contributor agreement")
    │        │ yes
    ├─ issue id linked?   ──no──→ BLOCK ("no linked issue")
    │        │ yes
    ├─ reviewers ≥ required? ─no─→ BLOCK ("needs N reviewers")
    │        │ yes
    ▼
  /integrate  → merge into mainline, formatted commit
    │
    ▼
  Result: NBI-1234 integrated (approved by Priya)

  Compare blocked paths:
    NewJoiner (no agreement) ──→ refused
    Rajesh (0 reviewers)     ──→ refused until review
```

  [OPENED] ─checks pass─→ [READY] ─/integrate─→ [INTEGRATED]
      │                       │
      │ check fails           │ review withdrawn
      ▼                       ▼
  [BLOCKED]               [NEEDS REVIEW]

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. integrate(good: NBI-1234, Rajesh, signed, [Priya])
  2.   canIntegrate → agreement ✓ → issue ✓ → reviewers 1≥1 ✓
  3.   → log "Integrated NBI-1234 by Rajesh"

sections.s6_takeaway:
Project Skara is the OpenJDK project that modernized how the JDK source code is stored and how contributions are reviewed. It migrated the codebase from Mercurial to Git, moved the repositories to GitHub, and built the automation that makes a pull-request workflow work under OpenJDK's governance. Before Skara, development used Mercurial with code review over mailing lists and webrev, which was unfamiliar and had a steep learning curve, so the barrier to entry was high. After Skara, a developer who already knows Git and GitHub can contribute using skills they already have.

The heart of Skara is the set of bots that reconcile an open pull-request workflow with OpenJDK's strict rules, because the project cannot simply accept any pull request. When you open a pull request, a bot checks that you have signed the contributor agreement so the change is legally clean, it verifies and links a valid issue in the JDK Bug System so every change is tracked, and it enforces the reviewer rules by confirming the required number of qualified reviewers have approved. When everything passes, the author comments the integrate command and the bot performs the formatted merge into the mainline. Skara also shipped command-line tools so contributors can run the same checks locally, and integrations for GitHub and GitLab.

Why it matters for contributors is the point I emphasize. The barrier to entry dropped because the workflow is now the familiar pull request almost every professional already knows. Review cycles got faster because the bots automate the clerical gatekeeping, so human reviewers spend their time on the actual code instead of process bookkeeping. I always add the senior framing that Skara is infrastructure and process, not a language or runtime feature, so it changes nothing about how my Java code behaves, but it matters strategically, because the long-term health of Java depends on attracting and retaining contributors, and a modern, automated, familiar workflow is a big part of that. In my own work at National Bank of India I applied the same idea to our internal shared-libraries platform, replacing an intimidating manual submission process with a pull-request flow plus automated gates for agreement, ticket linking, and reviewer count, and contributions and review speed both improved.
